title: Language anecdotes: French accent and Russian soldier
summary: Maxwell jokes about his French and Russian and says good English is clear thinking.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You sure made great use of it. That's unique among musicians, I'll tell you that. These stories you're telling me are just most interesting.
Well, most musicians, I find, are pretty interested in languages. I know in Europe they've all got a smattering.
I speak Spanish with a Mississippi accent.

Well, that's what they tell me in France. Every summer I go to the same restuarant and the woman says, "You haven't learned French yet, have you?" And I said, "You understand me." She said, "Yeah, you speak very fluently and you have the worst accent and the worst grammar." And I said, "Well, do you understand me?" She said, "Yes." I said, "Well, then, why tire myself out trying to perfect it."

I did the same thing with Russian. I figure the Russians don't speak their own language all that good. They've got thousands of endings on words so I always mumbled the ending on the word and nobody ever gave me any trouble about it. In fact, one time a Russian soldier asked me some directions and I said I was sorry, I wasn't Russian, I was American and he wouldn't believe me. I was so elated.
Yeah, I thought, oh, boy, I did pretty good.

It's fun, you know, to go to a foreign country. You want to communicate with the people and I don't want to go there and just sit around and talk to the Americans all the time. And if you can say a few words, it just makes it more fun. You know, maybe I know two or three hundred words but I know how to put them together. That's the interesting part about languages, how to put the words together. And with two or three hundred words, you can say anything, actually. We don't use that many in English.
(Inaudible) few thousand words in our vocabulary.

We don't need them, you know. Good English is just clear thinking. It's not a fancy word, it's being able to think clearly and put it simply. That's good English, not big words. I think that would apply to any language. At least that's the principle I used.
